items.prose: You hold 100 shares and want to sell them at once.
items.question: What price do you get per share?

options.why: That is the best ask, what a buyer pays. A seller gets the best bid.
That is the mid. Nobody is buying at the mid, so a sell now gets the best bid.
That is a deeper bid. The best bid, £20.00, has 900 shares, enough for your 100.

feedback.correct: A sell now gets the best bid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A seller trades with the highest waiting buyer.

explain.text: Selling now means trading with the best waiting buyer, at £20.00. Its 900 shares cover your 100, so every share gets £20.00.

items.prose: A small-cap has best bid £7.48 and best ask £7.52.
items.question: What is its spread in basis points? Give one decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the spread by the mid, then multiply by 10,000.

byKey.pence: 4 is the spread in pence. Divide by the £7.50 mid to compare shares.
byKey.bid: You divided by the best bid, £7.48. Divide by the mid, £7.50.
byKey.percent: That is the spread as a percentage. Multiply by 100 for basis points.

explain.text: The mid is £7.50 and the spread £0.04. $0.04 / 7.50 \times 10{,}000 = 53.3$ bp, more than 13 times the 4 bp of a £100 share with the same 4p gap.

items.prose: Asks: 300 shares at £20.00, then 500 at £20.02. You send a market buy for 800 shares.
items.question: What is your average price per share? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each price by its shares.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the two prices equally. 500 of the 800 shares paid £20.02.
byKey.best: Only 300 shares fill at £20.00. The order walks up to £20.02 for the rest.

explain.text: $300 \times 20.00 + 500 \times 20.02 = 16{,}010$. Divided by 800 that is £20.0125, five-eighths of the way to £20.02.

items.prose: Same order: 800 shares bought for £16,010. The best bid was £19.98 and the best ask £20.00 before you traded.
items.question: How much more did you pay than 800 shares at the mid, in £?

widget.label: Cost against the mid in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the mid, then compare with 800 shares at that price.

byKey.best-ask: £10 is against the best ask, £20.00. The mid is 1p lower, £19.99, which adds £8.
byKey.half: £8 is the half-spread alone: 1p on 800 shares. The walk adds £10.

explain.text: The mid is £19.99, so 800 shares at the mid cost £15,992. You paid £16,010, which is £18 more: £8 of half-spread and £10 from walking the book.

items.prose: At your bid price the line is: 500 shares, then 200, then 800, then your order. A trade of 600 shares prints at that price.
items.question: How many shares are ahead of you now?

feedback.correct: The trade cleared 600 shares from the front.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the traded shares off the front of the line.

byKey.unchanged: The trade filled orders ahead of you, so the line in front shrank.
byKey.filled: The trade was 600 shares, but 1,500 stood ahead of you. Your order is still waiting.

explain.text: The 600 shares fill the first order (500) and 100 of the second. That leaves 100 + 800 = 900 shares ahead of you.

items.prose: Your sell limit at £20.04 is second in line, behind 2,000 shares. A buyer now buys 1,500 shares at £20.04.
items.question: What happened to your order?

options.text: Nothing yet: it is now behind 500 shares
It sold, because a trade printed at its price
options.why: You assumed a trade at your price includes you. The 1,500 shares went to the order at the front.

options.text: Part of it sold, shared with the order in front
options.why: You split the trade across the line. Under price-time priority the front order takes it all first.

feedback.correct: The front order took all 1,500 shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Serve the line from the front.

explain.text: All 1,500 shares went to the order ahead of you, which still has 500 left. Your order moved up but holds no fill. A trade at your price is not a fill for you.

items.prose: A share has a 6p spread, so the half-spread is 3p. A limit at the bid fills with chance 0.7. A miss costs 4p a share against the mid.
items.question: What is the limit's expected cost, in pence a share against the mid?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each cost by its chance, keeping the sign of the saving.

byKey.sign: A filled bid saves 3p, so that cost is −3p. Keep the sign.
byKey.fill-only: You counted only the fill. With chance 0.3 the bid misses and costs 4p.
byKey.full-spread: That is the saving when it fills. Weight it by 0.7 and add the miss.

explain.text: $0.7 \times (-3) + 0.3 \times 4 = -2.1 + 1.2 = -0.9$p. The market order costs the half-spread, 3p, so the limit is cheaper on average here.

items.prose: Bids: 400 shares at £20.05, 300 at £20.02, 600 at £19.99. You send a sell limit for 900 shares at £20.00.
items.question: How many of your shares are left resting in the book?

widget.label: Shares left resting
widget.accept: 200: 400 and 300 trade at once; £19.99 is below your limit.

feedback.correct: 700 sell at once; 200 rest at £20.00 as the new best ask.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sell to every bid at or above £20.00, then see what is left.

byKey.all-fill: You let the order sell at £19.99. Your limit is £20.00, so it stops above that bid.
byKey.none: Bids at £20.05 and £20.02 are above your limit, so those shares trade at once.
byKey.market: You took the size of the bid at £19.99. Your order rests with what is left after 700 trade.

explain.text: The order is marketable down to £20.00: it sells 400 at £20.05 and 300 at £20.02. The bid at £19.99 is below the limit, so the last 200 rest at £20.00 and become the best ask.
